sentences.text: Hi, Carl, how you doing?
Hey, Andy, how are you?
I'm good, thank you.
I'm good.
We speak at last.
I think we've had to change this a couple of times.
We do.
There's definitely been at least one reschedule.
Sorry about that.
I'm sure you're very busy as well.
Yeah, well.
No, no, no problem, no problem.
So how shall we kick off?
Would you like to tell me a couple of minutes about Capital A and then I'll tell you a little bit about lfpr?
Yeah, sure, yeah.
I'd love to learn a little bit more about you, but of course I'm happy to tell you a bit more about Capital A.
So we are an M and A advisory.
We specialize in marketing services.
So mostly working with different types of agencies.
PR, communications, events, experiential, etc.
We help our clients to find the ideal buyers or acquisition targets.
We work both on the buy and the sell side.
And so, yeah, working with agencies.
This year we've done about 50 million in acquisition valuation already.
We have a network of buyers that are ready to engage with our sellers as well.
We have over 130,000 agencies in our CRM.
So, yeah, be really good to.
I didn't know there were 130,000 agencies in the world.
Well, there are more than that in the world because the majority of our CRM is actually the US with then probably about another 20%.
That's UK based, with a small bit of Australia, New Zealand and Europe, depending on some of the stuff we've done for other clients.
Yeah, so I'd say largely we don't really deal with Asia, so I should imagine there's probably another 130,000 out there somewhere.
Right, right.
Okay.
All right, well, that's really, really interesting.

I'll start by saying I think we're probably too small for you guys, but, you know, we were too small for results when we sold our agency in London at one time, and then a few years later we weren't anymore.
So let me, let me give you.
Before I talk about lfpr, let me give you a couple of minutes on my background, but more importantly my wife's background.
Leslie, back when I lived in London for 30 years, she's British and back when we were dating, she was the director of the Holmes and Merchant Group.
She ran their PR division and she.
This was, this was 1995 and she loved her job and her team and her clients, but she couldn't stand the old fashioned British public school, executive dining room culture of the group.
She was with.
And so we weren't married at that time, we were just dating.
But I said, well, why don't you, why don't you quit?
Why don't you start your own shop?
So the next week she quit her job and I put 50 grand in.
And that was in 1998.
And then it became HSD Communications, became the 14th largest healthcare agency in the UK and in 2007 we sold it to Gyro International.
That's back when Gyro International was something.
Today it's, it's been bought and it's been bought again and it's some little part of, of HSD is now part of Dentsu in Japan, you know, the mega, the mega agency in Japan.
So I think that's where ultimately wound up that agency turned over.
I mean it wasn't huge, but it was in dollars, about 4 or 5 million dollars turnover fee billings.
And Leslie focused mostly on health care.
She did, she started with a lot of medical devices because medical devices was sort of the low, a bastard stepchild of the healthcare industry back in the, in the 90s.
And so they didn't have the kind of budgets that pharma had.
And so she, she managed to get in there with, you know, Bard and Welsh, Allen and a number of those guys and ultimately she wound up doing a lot of P to Palm and OTC stuff.
She worked for all the, for Wreckit, Ben Keser.
She did all their, their consumer baby products.
And yeah, so it was largely a healthcare shop with a few other things in there.
Gyro, they were in, we didn't know it at the time, but they were in the process of selling their group to another group and they had everything except pr.
They had digital branding, advertising.
I mean you, they had everything except they had this big hole called pr.
And so we didn't realize they were buying our little agency in order to fill that hole six weeks before they sold to somebody else.
But anyway, it all worked out well for everybody.
So Leslie stayed with them for a year.
But there was a real culture clash.
I mean we knew, we knew it going in.

There was going to be a big culture clash because I don't, I don't know if you know anything about Gyro, but you know, I would call them sort of East End wide boy advertising guys, you know, duck and dive and bully and all that.
And Leslie was into healthcare PR with the big pharma companies and stuff where it's much more subtle and much softer approach and a lot of soft medical education and stuff.
Like that.
And so we knew it was probably going to be a train wreck in terms of culture, and it was.
But they offered three times more than the second bidder.
So culture clash or not, we sold it to Gyro and, and so then we moved.
We had a vacation home here in Savannah, Georgia and we'd had it for a few years.
But in about 2009 we came over here full time.
And Leslie, she retired after we sold hsd and so she swore she was going to retire at the, whatever it was, the ripe old age of 40.
And then she did a little charity work and she did a little more and then people started paying her to freelance and then she hired somebody and she hired somebody else.
And so today, even though our turnover is sub 1 million, I mean it's nudging right up at the 1 million mark.
It's Leslie Francis.
PR is still the largest marketing agency in, in southeastern Georgia.

Commercial business, a lot of small business and some not so small business.
A few national businesses as well.

Georgia Tech is one of her clients.

And government.

They got so big and successful they took it all in house.
But Bryan county is the fastest growing county in the United States, you may know.
And so victim of her own success over a six year, a six year run now she, she looks after a number of small municipals like the city of Port Wentworth as a big client.
She does a lot of grant funded opioid addiction and control work.
You know, there's a, there's a lot of money and sort of addiction control, stopping kids in high school from vaping and drugs and gateway stuff and everything else.
And so she, she manages a number of programs there.
And then there's the non profit stuff which is less today because it's all been a little bit, you know, they've been under budget cut.
She did both the, the good cause nonprofits and the cultural nonprofits as well.
And she still manages some of those.
The team is, is five full timers and about 10 freelancers that come and go on a 1099 basis.
And yeah, it's you know, it'll turn over probably a million bucks this year, and we probably getting.
When you include what Leslie gets out of it, probably got 30% margins on that.
So I would call it a profitable little business that's miles ahead of anybody else in this sort of million.
This greater Savannah area of perhaps a million people.
And she's probably double or triple the size of the next biggest agency.
So I'll stop.
I'll stop there.
And you can see why I said, you know, we're very proud of what she's got.
I mean, I do the books, and I work on it a few hours a week, but I'm not really involved in the business.
But you can see why.
I started by saying we're probably too small for you guys.

And so that's.

Yeah.

summary.overview: During the exploratory business meeting between Carl Francis and Andy Day, they discussed the potential sale of Leslie Francis PR, a marketing agency run by Carl's wife, Leslie. The meeting began with introductions and background information, highlighting that Capital A is an M&A advisory firm specializing in marketing services, having facilitated $50 million in acquisitions this year and managing a CRM with over 130,000 agencies. They noted the agency's current situation: Leslie, at 58, is considering the future of her business, which currently has a turnover nearing $1 million and lacks a strong sales presence. Capital A offered various services, including a free listing on their platform and a paid option promising buyer engagement within six months. As the meeting concluded, Carl expressed interest in exploring these options, planning to discuss them with Leslie, while Andy committed to sending an engagement letter and preparing a listing in hopes of going live before Thanksgiving. Action items were clearly delineated for both parties to facilitate the next steps.
